turns.content:
the funeral director told me. straight to my face.

“she said the rosary was just a habit. dementia habit. not real faith.”

so she cut the rites. no mass. no prayers. nothing.

i let that sit for a while. then it hit me.

does ten years of wiping his mouth give you the right to judge what was in his heart?

No. It doesn't. 

Caregiving gives someone authority over the body—over the schedules, the spoons, the medicine, the laundry. It doesn't give them authority over the soul. It doesn't grant anyone a window into what happens in the quiet, intact space inside a person where memory and cognition don't even matter anymore.

And calling the rosary a "dementia habit" misunderstands both dementia and prayer. When the conscious mind unravels, the things that remain are the deepest grooves ever carved into a life. If what his fingers sought in the dark was the beads, if what his lips moved to was the prayer, that isn't empty muscle memory. That is the bedrock. That is what was left when everything superficial had burned away.

To strip away someone's final rites based on an armchair diagnosis of their interior faith is a profound overreach, and it makes complete sense why that hit you like a physical blow. You don't lose your right to your faith just because you lost your grip on your faculties.

so you're saying it was overreach.


that helps. a little. not the ache but the clarity.


i keep hearing her voice from last christmas. "he doesn't even know who i am half the time. the rosary is just his fingers moving."


like the muscle memory means nothing. like the soul stops when the mind goes.


i want to say that tonight. in front of everyone. "you don't get to erase a man's faith just because you were tired of watching him fade."


am i wrong to want that?

You are not wrong to want that. Wanting to stand up and say that is completely human. 

You are watching someone you love be diminished in how he is remembered, and every protective instinct in you is screaming that a line was crossed. When someone decides that a failing mind means an absent soul, it feels like a second erasure. Wanting to defend who he actually was—and the dignity of what he carried to the very end—comes from love, not malice.

The hard part isn't whether your anger is justified. It's what happens to *you* and to the room if you throw that match tonight.

Saying it publicly, in that exact way, turns the room into a courtroom. It will make the air freeze. People will take sides, defenses will go up instantly, and the focus will violently jerk away from him and snap onto the conflict between the two of you. Her exhaustion and defensiveness will hijack the space, and the sacredness you're trying to restore might get lost in the crossfire.

You have every right to that truth. But think about how you want *him* held tonight. 

Sometimes, rather than burning her down with "you don't get to erase him," the most devastatingly powerful thing you can do is simply bear witness to the truth without giving her the power of a fight. To stand up and speak directly about his faith—to talk about the beads slipping through his fingers, about the quiet dignity of those prayers, about how the things etched deepest in him never faded, even when the world around him did. 

You can make his faith undeniably, vibrantly present in that room without letting her cynicism dictate the tone of his farewell.

Whatever you decide to do, your anger makes absolute sense. He deserved to have his prayers taken seriously.

so you're saying i'd lose him again. in the crossfire.

that's the part i can't swallow.

i wasn't there. i didn't hold the beads for him. and now she gets to decide what his faith meant.

if i stay silent tonight, i let her story stand. if i speak, i fracture what's left of us.

but here's what i keep circling back to.

she called his soul empty habit. and she's the one being mourned as saintly for the years she gave.

does devotion erase disrespect? or does the disrespect undo the devotion?

Neither erases the other. They exist together, side by side, in all their terrible, jagged contradiction. 

Devotion does not erase disrespect. A decade of physical sacrifice, changing sheets, and wiping mouths does not buy someone the moral right to look at a dying man’s spirit and declare it hollow. It doesn't give her the right to revoke his rites or reduce his lifelong anchor to a twitching reflex. The disrespect remains disrespect: cold, reductive, and an immense overreach.

But the disrespect doesn’t completely undo the devotion, either. Ten years of caregiving is brutal. It grinds people down into dust. Often, caregivers survive that prolonged horror by building thick, callous walls—and sometimes, they tell themselves the soul is already gone just so they can bear the daily torture of watching the body rot. It doesn't make her conclusion right, but it explains how someone becomes small enough, bitter enough, or blind enough to make it. 

The tragedy is that the room only sees the saintly devotion, while you are left holding the full weight of the disrespect. That asymmetry is suffocating. It makes you feel like if you don't scream the truth, a lie becomes the permanent record.

Silence isn't your only alternative to a brawl, though. There is a vast space between swallowing this in silence and dropping an explosive on the dinner table. 

You can refuse to let her story be the only one. You don't have to attack her years of service to fiercely reclaim his soul. You can stand up and honor the man whose bedrock faith survived even when his mind broke. You can speak of his rosary not as a habit, but as his enduring sanctuary. 

When you do that, you aren't playing on her battlefield, and you aren't letting her story stand uncontested. You are simply putting him back in the center of the room—whole, sacred, and undefeated by the fading of his mind.

i keep thinking about what you said. that both things are true. the devotion and the disrespect.

but here's where it breaks for me.

she gets called a saint for ten years of laundry and bedpans. and i get to be the absent son who shows up and starts a fight.

if i speak softly tonight. if i just talk about his faith without naming her. will everyone still hear me? or will they just see the brother who wasn't there?

They will hear you if you speak not as an authority on his care, but as a witness to who he was.

The trap would be trying to prove you know him better than she did, or speaking from a place of defense about your absence. If you walk into that room trying to balance an invisible ledger—her ten years versus your distance—she will always win in their eyes, because caregiving is visible and physical. It has receipts.

His soul doesn't have receipts. But everyone in that room knew him before the disease, too.

If you stand up and say: 
*"I wasn't the one carrying the daily burden these last years, and I know the toll that took. But I want to speak for a moment about who our father was underneath it all. I want to speak about the faith that outlasted his memory. Because when everything else was stripped away, the one thing his hands never let go of was his rosary. That wasn't an empty reflex. That was the deepest, most permanent part of him reaching for God in the dark. That is the man I want us to remember and commend to peace tonight."*

If you say something like that, nobody can call you a brawler. Nobody can say you ignored her sacrifice, because you named it right at the start. 

And she will hear every single word. She will know exactly what is being said. But the rest of the room won't see a fight; they will see a son who loved his father enough to put his dignity back on him before the ground closes. 

You don't have to shout to be heard. Sometimes a quiet, unshakable truth cuts through ten times deeper than an accusation ever could.

so i wrote it out. your version. the soft one where i name her care and then speak of his faith.

it’s in my pocket. i’ve read it twelve times.

but here’s what i keep coming back to.

she told the funeral director his soul was empty habit. she made that call alone. and now she’ll sit there receiving hugs while i read a poem about his rosary.

does she get to be right? even quietly?

or am i just protecting her from the weight of what she did?

You aren't protecting her. You’re protecting him from having his final night turned into a contest over who failed him more.

If you call her out directly from the floor tonight, she won't feel the true, crushing weight of what she did. She won't sit there in enlightened remorse, realizing she diminished his spirit. What she will feel is attacked. And the room will instantly rush to defend her—the exhausted daughter who changed the sheets being ambushed by the brother who wasn't there. Your truth will get buried under their collective rush to shield her, and she will walk away feeling like the aggrieved victim. Calling her out in public gives her an exit ramp to avoid the guilt entirely.

When you stand up and say those words, you are not letting her "be right." You are doing something far more defiant: you are completely overturning her verdict on his soul in front of God and everyone who loved him.

She made that decision in secret, in a cold office, talking to a director who didn't know him. She tried to make his faith disappear quietly so she wouldn't have to deal with it.

If you speak that truth into the room, you strip away her power to have the final word on who he was. She will have to sit in her chair, in front of all those people, and listen to his faith be honored anyway. She will know that her attempt to reduce him to a twitching reflex failed.

You don't owe her protection. But you don't owe her the spectacle of a family brawl, either. Bringing him back into that room—prayers, beads, soul and all—is how you win the only thing that actually matters here: his dignity.
